key_facts: **Scarlet fever** is a group A streptococcal (*S. pyogenes*) infection with a toxin-mediated rash; commonest in children aged 2–8.
Sore throat, fever, then a **sandpaper** rash (neck, chest, flexures), flushed cheeks with **circumoral pallor**, **strawberry tongue**, Pastia lines.
**Phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days**; clarithromycin or azithromycin if penicillin allergic.
**Notifiable**; exclude from school or work until 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
Watch for **invasive group A strep** (iGAS): fever with severe illness, spreading cellulitis, necrotising signs: same-day emergency care.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A toxin-mediated illness caused by **group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus** (*Streptococcus pyogenes*, GAS), usually after **streptococcal pharyngitis/tonsillitis** (occasionally a skin/wound source). Mainly children **2–10 years**; peaks in winter/spring. Notable UK surges (e.g. 2014–2018, winter 2022–23 with rise in invasive GAS). **Strawberry tongue** = inflamed, enlarged fungiform papillae on the dorsum of the tongue.

sub: Children 2–8 years in winter and spring; outbreaks in schools and nurseries.
UK outbreaks rose sharply in 2022–23 with more iGAS.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact (incubation 2–5 days). GAS strains producing **streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA/B/C — superantigens)** cause the diffuse rash and enanthem; immunity is toxin-specific, so second episodes are possible. Complications arise by local spread (suppurative), immune mechanisms (non-suppurative), or invasion (iGAS).

ul: Streptococcal **pyrogenic exotoxins** (SpeA, SpeC) act as superantigens.
**"Scarlet fever is a disease of the past"**: it is common again in the UK.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The rash is caused by **toxins**, not by bacteria in the skin.

mech.t: GAS infects the throat or tonsils (occasionally skin or wounds).
Pyrogenic exotoxins act as **superantigens**, activating many T cells non-specifically.
Cytokines dilate dermal capillaries, giving the fine sandpaper erythema, flushed face and strawberry tongue.
mech.caption: Flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor.

mech.t: Peeling of fingertips and toes after 1–2 weeks.

histo: Not needed. Throat swab for culture or rapid antigen test supports diagnosis (UKHSA).

ul: Abrupt **fever**, **sore throat** (exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical nodes), headache, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain.

Rash after 12–48 h: **fine, pinhead, "sandpaper" erythema** starting on neck/chest, spreading to trunk/limbs; blanches; **Pastia lines** (linear petechial accentuation in skin folds — antecubital, axillae); **flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor**. On darker skin the rash may be hard to see but **feels rough**.
**Tongue:** day 1–2 **"white strawberry tongue"** (white coat with red papillae poking through) → day 3–5 **"red strawberry/raspberry tongue"** (coat sheds). Palatal petechiae (Forchheimer spots).
Rash fades in ~1 week, followed by **desquamation** of fingertips, toes, groin.

**Causes of strawberry tongue:** scarlet fever; **Kawasaki disease**; **toxic shock syndrome** (staph or strep); also reported with vitamin B12/folate deficiency (glossitis), yellow fever, allergy/drug reactions and some other infections.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: **Clinical** in primary care (UKHSA). Throat swab for culture (or rapid antigen test where available) if uncertain or in outbreaks/closed settings. Not routinely needed before treatment. If unwell: FBC, CRP, blood cultures, ASO titre (retrospective).

ul: Diagnose clinically in primary care (UKHSA).
Culture or rapid antigen if uncertain or outbreaks.
FBC, CRP, blood cultures; ASO retrospectively.

ddx.name: Kawasaki disease
ddx.f: **Fever ≥ 5 days**, conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen then peeling hands / feet; < 5 years: urgent paediatrics.

ddx.name: SSSS
ddx.f: Tender erythema, flaccid blisters, Nikolsky +, no tonsillitis.

ddx.name: Viral exanthems
ddx.f: Measles (coryza, cough, Koplik), slapped cheek; no sandpaper texture.

sections.title: Management
blocks: Based on UKHSA *Guidelines for the public health management of scarlet fever* and NICE CKS *Scarlet fever*:

blocks.h: First-line antibiotics (to speed recovery, reduce transmission and complications)

ul: **Phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days** (BNF age-banded doses; e.g. adults/children ≥12 years 500 mg four times daily, or 1 g twice daily per local guidance).

Penicillin allergy: **clarithromycin** (5 days) or **azithromycin** (per BNF/local guidance); **amoxicillin** (10 days) is an alternative where liquid palatability/supply is an issue (follow UKHSA/local advice during shortages).
Complete the full course.
**Notifiable disease** in England & Wales — the diagnosing registered medical practitioner notifies UKHSA (pharmacist prescribers should ensure this happens via the GP/local process).
**Exclusion:** children and adults stay off school/nursery/work **until 24 hours after starting antibiotics**; untreated cases are infectious for ~2–3 weeks.
Outbreaks (≥2 cases in a setting within 10 days) → inform local Health Protection Team; extra caution if chickenpox co-circulating (iGAS risk).
Hygiene: hand washing, cover coughs, don't share cutlery/towels.
Paracetamol/ibuprofen for fever and throat pain (avoid ibuprofen if dehydrated or chickenpox co-infection per local advice), fluids, soft foods, emollient for itch/peeling.

NHS **Pharmacy First** (England) acute sore throat pathway uses FeverPAIN for pharyngitis; check the current pathway on how suspected scarlet fever is handled (typically outside PGD scope → prescriber/GP).

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Chickenpox in the household**: Higher iGAS risk: lower threshold for review.
**Safety-net**: In writing, for iGAS; dark urine or swelling 1–3 weeks later.

refer.t: Rapid deterioration, severe pain, spreading skin infection, breathing difficulty, sepsis: **invasive GAS**.
Fever ≥ 5 days with red eyes, red lips, swollen hands / feet: consider **Kawasaki disease**.
Dark urine or swelling 1–3 weeks later: check urine (post-strep nephritis).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Rapid deterioration, severe pain, a spreading skin infection, breathing difficulty or signs of sepsis: **invasive GAS**, emergency.
Fever for 5 days or more with red eyes, red lips, swollen hands and feet: consider **Kawasaki disease**.
Chickenpox plus scarlet fever in the same household: higher invasive GAS risk, so lower threshold for review.

blocks.h4: Red flags / refer — **safety-net for invasive GAS**

ul: Same-day / 999: persistent high fever despite antipyretics, drowsiness, confusion, severe muscle pain, rapidly spreading painful red skin (necrotising fasciitis), difficulty breathing, dehydration, signs of sepsis/shock (NICE NG51).
Quinsy (trismus, uvula deviation), otitis media, sinusitis, cervical abscess, pneumonia.

Late: **acute rheumatic fever** (2–4 weeks; arthritis, carditis), **post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis** (1–3 weeks; dark urine, oedema, hypertension), **PANDAS** (rare), and the link to **guttate psoriasis**.
Features of Kawasaki (fever ≥5 days, conjunctivitis) or TSS (hypotension) → urgent.
Otitis media, quinsy, sinusitis, pneumonia.
**iGAS**: necrotising fasciitis, sepsis, toxic shock.
Late: rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Recovers within a week with antibiotics.

pearls: "Sandpaper rash + sore throat + strawberry tongue + circumoral pallor" = scarlet fever until proven otherwise; on darker skin rely on texture and the tongue.
Strawberry tongue is **not specific** — a child with ≥5 days of fever and red eyes needs Kawasaki excluded.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin is best taken on an empty stomach; four-times-daily dosing needs adherence support (use bd regimen where appropriate).
Tell parents peeling of fingers/toes 1–2 weeks later is expected.
Safety-net clearly and in writing for iGAS symptoms; advise urine check/return if dark urine or swelling after 1–3 weeks.

quiz.q: When can the child return to school?
Strawberry tongue and 6 days of fever with conjunctivitis?
quiz.a: Consider Kawasaki disease: urgent paediatric referral.
